D  Acommittee was set up to develop the cycle way and apply for funding from the
government. Then a plan was submitted and an agreement signed. Construction of the
trail began in January 2011 and by the end of 2013, the trail was fully signposted and
open to cyclists. Jason Gaskill, Tourism Board general manager, says it has been great
to see this project come to life. However, to develop a project of this size inevitably

to towns and urban areas. Further work is planned to better incorporate other townships
and provide a more scenic riding experience. Minimising accidents and risk is a priority,
and the public have communicated that they want more off-road trails so they are
separated from traffic.
More support services have developed as a result of the growing number of cyclists in
the area. One of these takes the form of organised tours with a knowledgeable guide
who can give information about the area on the way. The relationship between
businesses in the area and the developers of the trail has boosted the economy and
produced a better overall riding experience. For example, riders can carry their own
luggage or have it delivered to their accommodation, which means you don't have to
carry the extra weight on your bike. Staff at the tourist information office on the Alps 2
Ocean Cycle Trail can provide all cyclists with a complimentary map so they don't need
to buy one. This includes lots of information about all sorts of different aspects of the
trail. Bikes are available for hire at the tourist information office and an additional
service has just been set up whereby staff can now provide riders with clothing they
might need on the trip for a small fee. If you go online, there are also regular updates
about the weather for each section of the trail, which is important as it is quite
changeable in this part of the country.
